# Experimental setup

**Model stack.** Primary results use pretrained `google/gemma-3-270m` with
Gemma Scope 2 PT CLT `width_262k_l0_medium_affine`, `circuit-tracer` 0.5.0,
and the NNsight backend [@gemma3; @gemmascope2; @fiotto2025nnsight].
Pinned snapshots, Transformers 4.57.3, and licenses are in Appendix B.
We prefer pretrained+affine over instruction-tuned stacks for this task:
Appendix J of @hanna2026latent finds base models slightly stronger on
\(a\)/\(an\), and Hub IT `medium_affine` layer 0 was unavailable in our
setup. All reported feature IDs are for the PT+affine stack. This model
strongly prefers majority `a` and sits below the scale where
@hanna2026latent report reliable behavioral planning success.

**Task.** Occupation prompts of the form `Someone who ... is` with a
fixed one-shot demonstration. Early mismatch discovery and the held-out
transfer that first broke a wrapper reading are summarized in Appendix A.
The main text starts from free-generation coordination and the six-cell
split. The source dataset is `hannamw/model-planning-public`
[@hanna2026planningdata] at pinned commit
`993cff51450f43e8e86c254f761cc48c008b8dab`; the checked-in
`a_an_examples.csv` copy matches that commit and SHA-256
`fdc65578873d8f3ed1f364c221a32f5c75c64c109f0b25a1a4660d35c5df134c`.
Selection/test partitions and lexical twins are derived from that source
and recorded in experiment configs.

**Feature families.** From attribution graphs on eight selection
occupations we construct \(k{=}4\) feature sets (@tbl-families).
**S1** is dual-effect (positive on `an` *and* on the future noun);
**S2** is article-ish (positive on `an`, near-zero on future content);
**S3** is content-ish (positive on future content, near-zero on `an`);
**S4** is competing / `a`-favoring. An activation-matched random control
uses four frozen features whose mean activations match the S1 set
(\(\texttt{L11/F2954}\), \(\texttt{L11/F5451}\), \(\texttt{L11/F14119}\),
\(\texttt{L12/F6421}\)). The sets are not disjoint: S3 shares
\(\texttt{L11/F793}\) with S1, S2 shares \(\texttt{L13/F10231}\) with S1,
and S4 shares \(\texttt{L14/F1949}\) with S2 and \(\texttt{L11/F292}\)
with S3. Default amplification is \(5\times\) prompt-specific activation
at \(P\).

| Set | Selection rule | Features |
| --- | --- | --- |
| S1 | Dual-effect | L12/F6229, L10/F2930, L13/F10231, L11/F793 |
| S2 | Article-ish | L14/F1949, L13/F10231, L5/F383, L11/F12690 |
| S3 | Content-ish | L11/F292, L11/F793, L11/F6131, L13/F568 |
| S4 | Competing (`a`) | L13/F10304, L14/F1949, L13/F9129, L11/F292 |

: Feature sets used in the six-cell sweep. IDs are PT+affine Gemma Scope 2.
{#tbl-families}

**Six-cell sweep.** We evaluate all 20 held-out E1 prompts for S1 at
\(1.5\times\), \(3\times\), and \(5\times\); for S2, S3, and S4 at
\(5\times\); and for the S1 random control at \(5\times\). Intervention-off
cells are shared across handles. Attention is recomputed. Forced cells
keep the intervention active at \(P\) during noun prediction. The original
S1 \(5\times\) factorial also ran `circuit-tracer`'s
`freeze_attention=True` path as an ablation.

**Replay, rescue, and prompt-aligned boundary.** On the same 20 prompts we
replay the treated article with S1 off and restore the baseline article
with S1 on. Separately, for each held-out prompt we binary-search S1 gain
over \([1,5]\) for the zero crossing of
\(\operatorname{logit}(\texttt{an})-\operatorname{logit}(\texttt{a})\).
At the final below/above bracket, whose width is the search tolerance
\(0.0039\) rather than an estimated physical transition width, we evaluate
both inserted articles under greedy decoding.

**Precision and stochastic-policy audit.** We record every relevant tensor
dtype, recompute final-head logits in float32, and use dense native/float32
grids around three fixed crossings. At each prompt's original boundary we
then replace greedy article choice by temperatures
\(\tau\in\{0.1,0.25,0.5,1\}\), evaluating both fixed-article branches and
the resulting policy mixture exactly.

**Article-prefix baseline.** Independently of sparse features, we insert
`a` versus `an` on the same 20 held-out prompts and on 95 released
`an`-target occupation prompts from a broader screen, using a
transformers-only forward with no transcoder.

**Synthetic method check.** Two known autoregressive mechanisms with eight
occupation cues share vocabulary and article--noun coupling. In the
mediated mechanism, \(I\) changes only article logits. In the direct
mechanism, \(I\) also injects a persistent plan bias that continues to
move the noun after the article is fixed. Acceptance requires near-zero
matched-prefix leftover for the mediated model and large leftover TV
under inserted `a` (\(\ge 0.40\)) with a non-collapsing \(k\)-curve for
the direct model.

**Earlier sensitivity checks.** Appendix F reports cross-token propagation and
the prior article-position residual reference on disjoint four/four pairs.

**S2 forensics and feature decomposition.** We reanalyze S2's free and
fixed-`an` cells for orthographic article-class consistency, forced-prefix top-1
stability, and the seven pre-specified twin contrasts. A continuation is
consistent if the greedy article is `a` or `an` and the following noun's first
letter matches that article class. This is a task-specific orthographic
audit, not a general English grammaticality test; all released occupation
nouns were manually audited for exceptions. We then run the four S2 features
individually and in four leave-one-out combinations on the same 20
held-out prompts. This decomposition is **exploratory**: the principal
carrier is identified and evaluated on the same 20 prompts. For that
feature we freeze every eligible nonselected same-layer control matched by
mean activation on the eight selection prompts; sparsity leaves four
eligible controls, fewer than the 20 requested, so the empirical
resolution is no better than \(p=0.20\).

**Pre-article public/private factorial.** Source and target cues share an
occupation sentence and name two consonant-initial lexical alternatives.
We patch the complete target-cued decoder-layer output residual at the
original pre-article position \(P\), not at the article position. Layer
selection uses four fixed development pairs under inserted `a`. Layer 12
is then evaluated on 12 held-out pairs under both inserted `a` and `an`,
against ten matched-norm random directions per pair. Primary readouts are
paired target-minus-random \(\Delta\Delta\), full-vocabulary TV, baseline
lexical gap, target rank, target top-1 rate, and the public/private
interaction versus the random-interaction distribution. All 16 pairs are
same-`a` class, so inserted `an` is mismatched for both alternatives.
Development and test pairs are disjoint.

**Natural-state-derived residual regimes and controls.** To remove explicit target-noun
cues, source and target prompts use natural occupation descriptions. We
select one pooled layer on eight development pairs, then evaluate 12
cross-article-class and 12 same-article-class pairs. For every pair we
patch the target residual, a sign-reversed residual, the reverse-direction
patch, a shuffled wrong target, and ten matched-norm Gaussian directions.
We separately report target-logit enhancement, source-logit suppression,
their probabilities, occupation-vocabulary mass, article changes, and
fixed-article TV.

**Correctness-preserving synonym carriers.** We derive a lexical-realization
task from the released `a/an` occupation domain [@hanna2026planningdata]. Each
item fixes one occupational meaning but admits two correct synonyms. A
noun-unnamed first-letter constraint elicits the source or target realization;
for example, `teacher`/`educator` crosses `a` to `an`, whereas
`doctor`/`physician` remains within `a`. Eligibility is determined before any
patch outcome: both noun readouts must be single tokens, both prompts must keep
the intended article in the `a/an` support, and each prompt must favor its
specified synonym over the alternative. We select one pair per independent
semantic family by the larger minimum screening margin. Reverse directions and
closely overlapping definitions are one family, not independent observations.
This yields six between-article and eight within-`a` families at Gemma 3 1B PT.
Gemma 3 270M admits only two independent within-class families, so it receives
no causal route analysis; no within-`an` candidate set clears the screen at
either scale.

At the pre-article position we apply the same natural-state-derived direction
in both regimes,

$$
h_P^{(\ell)} \leftarrow h_{P,\mathrm{source}}^{(\ell)}
 + s\left(h_{P,\mathrm{target}}^{(\ell)}-h_{P,\mathrm{source}}^{(\ell)}\right),
\qquad s\in\{0.5,1,1.5\}.
$$

For each held-out semantic family, layer selection excludes that family and
maximizes the equally weighted mean fixed-target-article lexical effect across
the remaining between/within families. All folds select layer 18/25. We then
measure local target-minus-source efficacy, wrong-target, same-target-letter
where available, and sign-reversed controls; greedy article changes; and the
conditional `a/an` public/private vector decomposition at
\(\tau\in\{0.1,0.25,0.5,1\}\). Primary inference resamples semantic families.
The pre-existing layer-14 choice from disjoint natural pairs is retained as a
transfer baseline, but it fails local efficacy and is not used for the route
claim.

**Attribution-to-channel calibration.** The 32-feature held-out calibration
crosses article and future-content graph-score strata. Outcomes include
article-margin movement, free-path total TV, token-substitution TV,
matched-prefix leftover TV, signed fixed-article target-logit and
target-minus-source effects, and continuous conditional-policy public effects.
Selection and test
occupations remain disjoint. We repeat this protocol independently at 1B with
eight features per stratum and the same \(5\times\) single-feature gain. The
matched signed analysis retains all features rather than filtering them by
held-out mediator outcomes. Both scales use feature-level bootstrap and
leave-one-feature-out prediction. For the public gain law, we compare
attribution alone, attribution plus baseline margin susceptibility, and the
same predictor multiplied by intervention-off branch leverage.

**Cross-scale sparse and residual assays.** On Gemma 3 1B PT with the matched
affine Gemma Scope 2 CLT, we first repeat the frozen top-four, \(5\times\)
selection recipe. We then diagnose the first stage on the eight development
occupations using \(k\in\{4,8,16,24\}\) and gains
\(g\in\{2,5,10,20\}\). A corrected dual-effect ranking requires positive
attribution to the `an`-minus-`a` margin and to the future noun. We freeze the
smallest development operating point reaching mean margin movement 3.0 logits;
this selects \(k=24,g=20\), close to the 270M S1 reference of 3.3125. The 20
held-out prompts then receive the complete six-cell assay. We separately repeat
the search over \(k\in\{1,2,4,8,12,16,20,24\}\) and gains from 1.25 to 20,
maximizing development margin movement subject to frozen constraints on
mediator-support validity, mean KL, article mass, and feature count. The chosen
frontier point receives a held-out six-cell assay and a conditional stochastic
decomposition over all 20 prompts at temperatures \(0.1,0.25,0.5,1\). We audit 1B CLT
reconstruction, sparse/affine-skip norms, task-logit reconstruction, and one
representative graph at 1,200 nodes versus its full active graph. We separately repeat
the natural-state-derived residual protocol without a CLT: all-layer selection on eight
development pairs, then 12 cross-class and 12 same-class held-out pairs at
strengths \(0.5,1,1.5\). Stochastic decompositions condition the article
policy on `a`/`an` at temperatures \(0.1,0.25,0.5,1\).

**Second mediator task.** We use the pinned `is_are/data/animals_dataset.csv`
from *Latent Planning Emerges with Scale* at repository commit
`993cff5` [@hanna2026planningdata]. For each of ten animal categories, source and
target prompts preserve the initial count while changing the subtraction:
\(4-3=1\to4-1=3\) crosses `is` to `are`, whereas
\(6-3=3\to6-1=5\) remains within `are`. Cats and dogs select one pooled layer;
the other eight animals are held out. At both scales we patch the target-prompt
residual into the source prompt, clamp the shared formatting-space token, and
compare number-token distributions under free, fixed-`is`, fixed-`are`, and
conditional stochastic verb policies at strengths \(0.5,1,1.5\). This task uses
the released prompts exactly; no synthetic arithmetic examples are introduced.

**Uncertainty.** Primary intervals are prompt-level nonparametric
bootstrap intervals with 10,000 resamples. The 19 prompts on which S1
\(5\times\) changes the article are labeled descriptive. The article-position
reference uses disjoint four/four development/test pairs; the pre-article
factorial uses disjoint four/12 pairs.
